title: A radically accessible, resilient anesthesia platform for essential surgery

concept.text: The proposed innovation is an affordable, maintainable anesthesia platform that makes the entire pathway dependable in settings with limited infrastructure: patient assessment, anesthetic delivery, ventilation, monitoring, recognition of complications, rescue and recovery. The platform would combine equipment, clinical workflows, training, maintenance and dependable access to necessary supplies. Its defining capability would be sustained safe operation within realistic staffing, power, oxygen and supply constraints.

This is a proposed systems capability. A resilient delivery device would be one component; establishing the broader platform would require showing that assessment, monitoring, rescue, recovery and ongoing support remain dependable together. The supplied material does not establish that the integrated goal has been achieved, or that it remains unmet across the field at the review’s November 1, 2026 reference date.

significance.text: As a conditional assessment, reliably delivering and monitoring anesthesia with minimal infrastructure could remove an important practical constraint on where essential operations can be performed. If affordability and sustained local operation were demonstrated alongside clinical performance, the platform could make surgical services more dependable in constrained hospitals and support care during infrastructure disruptions or disasters.

Broader surgical access would be a possible downstream consequence, rather than an automatic result. It would still require surgical staff, suitable facilities, medicines, referral systems and financing. An evaluation would therefore need to distinguish improved anesthesia capability from an actual increase in timely, affordable surgical care. The supplied evidence does not quantify the potential population benefit.

The potentially revolutionary feature is dependable delivery of a complete service under difficult operating conditions. That achievement could arise from engineering, clinical integration and implementation rather than a fundamental scientific discovery. Infrastructure resilience also cannot be assumed to make every operation or patient suitable for the same setting; appropriate case selection and access to escalation would remain part of the proposed capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed capability gap is reliable integration across the anesthesia pathway. Delivery, monitoring, ventilation, complication recognition, rescue and recovery must work as a coordinated service, including when power, oxygen or other supplies become unreliable. The supplied record identifies this as the candidate breakthrough but does not establish which parts are currently unavailable, how widely existing solutions are deployed, or whether a complete implementation already exists.

Engineering synthesis: concrete barriers include defining tolerable interruption conditions, maintaining clinically adequate performance during those interruptions, making degradation recognizable to staff, and providing workable escalation and rescue options. Resilience must be assessed across the assembled system: a delivery component that continues operating does not by itself establish that monitoring, ventilation or recovery support remains adequate.

Implementation synthesis: affordability and maintainability require more than a low purchase price. The proposed platform would need an achievable staffing and training model, locally workable servicing, replacement parts and consumables, and a supply chain that supports sustained use. These are interdependent constraints: a technically capable system can still fail its intended purpose if it cannot be staffed, repaired or replenished. The supplied material does not establish their costs or feasibility.

A further barrier is defining the clinical scope precisely enough to evaluate safety. A broad essential-surgery case mix needs explicit patient, procedure and setting boundaries. Outcome comparisons must account for differences in baseline risk and available support, so that favorable results from a selected population are not treated as evidence of general suitability.

current_state.text: The reconciled research attributes a partial demonstration to Stefani A. Vande Lune and colleagues in “Universal Anesthesia Machine: Clinical Application in an Austere, Resource-Limited Environment,” published online December 28, 2019, in the May–June 2020 issue of Military Medicine, DOI 10.1093/milmed/usz438. It describes use of a draw-over Universal Anesthesia Machine in 20 patients in Haiti where external oxygen and reliable electricity were limited. These details are retained as the supplied research’s account of the report; they were not independently confirmed by the evidence review.

The research states that only an abstract or minimal publisher record was available during its pass and that the full text was not inspected. The source index contains no captured document artifacts, and the review received no abstract or article text. Consequently, the review could not verify the reported sample, setting, draw-over operation, infrastructure conditions or study design. This is a limitation on verification, not evidence that the report or its stated findings are false.

If the supplied description is accurate, the 20-patient report provides a limited clinical example of resilient anesthetic delivery. Such a small observational report would not establish sustained performance across a broad essential-surgery case mix, integration of the complete pathway, long-term local maintainability, comparative patient outcomes or population-scale improvements in access. Those broader capabilities cannot be inferred from the reported device use.

No newer evidence or usable freshness search record was supplied. The dated report therefore cannot establish the state of the field as of November 1, 2026, or the task date. The remaining uncertainty concerns both the cited demonstration’s verified scope and whether subsequent work has achieved the integrated goal.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: independently evaluated deployments across diverse low-resource and disaster settings would show sustained use for a prespecified period and a defined, broad essential-surgery case mix. The evaluation would state patient and procedure eligibility, exclusions, staffing, infrastructure and available referral support. These are proposed criteria for convincing evidence, not established consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Independent evaluations demonstrate sustained essential surgery across diverse settings

completion_criteria.text: Proposed resilience assessment: deployments would demonstrate reliable operation during specified power, oxygen and other supply interruptions, with the duration and severity of those interruptions reported. Evaluators would examine the whole pathway, including monitoring, ventilation, recognition of deterioration, escalation, rescue and recovery. They would document failures, workarounds and circumstances requiring postponement, transfer or higher levels of support.
completion_criteria.label: The whole anesthesia pathway operates reliably during specified supply interruptions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical assessment: patient outcomes would meet prespecified, clinically justified comparison criteria against an appropriate adequately resourced standard, accounting for case mix and baseline risk. Outcome definitions and acceptable comparison margins would need justification before evaluation. Successful equipment operation alone would not establish comparable clinical outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Risk-adjusted patient outcomes meet prespecified clinically justified comparison criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical and reproducibility assessment: independent teams would reproduce sustained performance across multiple sites, including sites operating through routine local staffing and maintenance arrangements. Reports would include total cost, training requirements, staffing, downtime, repair needs, replacement parts, consumables, supply failures and actual changes in surgical access. Follow-up would test whether performance persists beyond the initial deployment period.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce sustained performance under routine local arrangements

completion_criteria.text: Successful finite evaluations would establish demonstrated breadth within the tested patients, procedures, sites and interruption conditions. They would not establish suitability for every operation, patient or disaster. A convincing completion claim would publish practical boundaries, remaining dependencies and conditions in which the platform requires additional resources or referral.
completion_criteria.label: Published boundaries identify dependencies and conditions requiring additional support

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ANS-01, “A causal theory of anesthetic-induced unconsciousness,” addresses explanatory science, whereas ANS-05 addresses dependable service delivery. ANS-02, “A reliable real-time monitor of conscious experience during anesthesia,” could contribute a monitoring capability, but its availability would not establish the broader pathway. ANS-05 does not itself resolve either the causal theory or the reliable measurement of conscious experience.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-03, “A broadly applicable, pain-selective surgical nerve block,” and ANS-04, “Surgical unconsciousness with preserved breathing and circulatory control,” concern specific anesthetic capabilities that could potentially reduce some demands on a constrained service. Each has a separate physiological objective. ANS-05 would still need to establish dependable delivery, monitoring, rescue and recovery for its defined clinical scope.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-06, “Broad, active reversal of general anesthesia,” could contribute to recovery or rescue. ANS-08, “Reliable rescue oxygenation in the difficult airway,” overlaps directly with emergency rescue capability. Neither would establish the complete resilient platform, and demonstrating ANS-05 within a defined scope would not establish broad reversal or universally reliable difficult-airway rescue.

Roster-based synthesis: ANS-07, “Systemic, non-opioid analgesia for severe perioperative pain,” ANS-09, “Mechanism-based prevention of chronic postsurgical pain,” and ANS-10, “Mechanism-guided anesthesia to prevent postoperative brain dysfunction,” address distinct treatment or prevention goals. They could inform the platform’s clinical protocols and outcomes, but dependable access to anesthesia would not by itself demonstrate these capabilities. ANS-05 retains its separate focus on integration, infrastructure resilience, maintainability and affordability.

unresolved_issues: The cited report’s abstract and full text were not supplied as captured artifacts; its exact design, outcomes, operating conditions and technical capabilities remain unverified in this record.
No usable freshness record establishes whether the integrated goal remained unmet as of November 1, 2026, or the task date.
The intended essential-surgery case mix, patient exclusions, deployment duration and tolerated interruption conditions require operational definitions.
Clinical outcome measures, comparison margins and the appropriate adequately resourced comparator require prospective justification.
Total cost, feasible staffing and training, local repair capacity, supply requirements and actual effects on access remain unquantified.
Whether the central obstacle requires new scientific knowledge, new engineering capabilities or primarily integration and implementation remains unresolved.

brief.title: Dependable surgical care where resources are scarce
possible: Patients could receive dependable anesthesia—the medicines and care that prevent pain during surgery—even where power, oxygen and supplies are unreliable. Hospitals could support them from assessment through recovery, with monitoring and help for breathing or complications.
Local teams could keep this service running with affordable equipment, practical training, repairs and dependable supplies.
why: Hospitals with limited resources could offer essential operations more dependably. Care could also continue through infrastructure failures and disasters.

sources.who: Stefani A. Vande Lune and colleagues
sources.showed: A small observational report describes use of an anesthesia machine in Haiti where oxygen and reliable electricity were limited.
sources.cited_for: The report describes clinical use under difficult infrastructure conditions.
sources.not_established: A small clinical report cannot establish dependable care across the full pathway or sustained local operation.

sources.showed: In an observational study in Sierra Leone, clinicians shifted from ketamine, an anesthetic drug given through a vein, to inhalational anesthesia, delivered as gas. The machine maintained anesthesia delivery during power cuts.
sources.quote: We observed a shift from the use of ketamine total intravenous anesthesia to inhalational anesthesia.
sources.cited_for: An anesthesia machine can maintain delivery through power failures in clinical use.
sources.not_established: The study does not establish comparable patient outcomes or reliability across the whole care pathway.

sources.showed: An oxygen-storage prototype supplied oxygen through most power outages during a test without patients in Uganda. It covered only part of the total time without power.
sources.quote: cover over 99% of power outage events over the course of the study.
sources.cited_for: Stored oxygen can bridge power failures that interrupt oxygen production.
sources.not_established: The prototype still needs clinical testing and cannot cover every interruption.

sources.showed: In Malawi, training accompanied donated pulse oximeters, devices that measure blood oxygen. Knowledge improved, and recorded episodes of low blood oxygen became less frequent as providers used them.
sources.quote: The pulse oximeters were in routine use 8 months after donation.
sources.cited_for: Monitoring equipment paired with training can remain in use and support safer anesthesia practice.
sources.not_established: This monitoring programme does not establish the reliability or patient outcomes of a complete anesthesia service.

shown: At Connaught Hospital in Sierra Leone, Sampson and colleagues observed gas anesthesia delivered in 287 cases with the Universal Anaesthesia Machine. Delivery continued during power cuts by switching to room air. This was an observational study at a single hospital.
missing: The whole service still needs to demonstrate reliable monitoring, breathing support, complication rescue and recovery through specified interruptions.
Patient outcomes still need comparisons that account for differences in patients’ health and operations.
Independent deployments still need to establish lasting affordability, local staffing, repairs and supplies, alongside effects on access to surgery.

milestones.label: Independent evaluations demonstrate sustained surgery across diverse settings
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluations would have to show sustained care across varied low-resource and disaster settings, with defined patients, operations and support. This would establish the breadth of dependable use.

milestones.label: The whole care pathway withstands specified supply interruptions
milestones.explanation: Deployments would have to maintain delivery, monitoring, breathing support, rescue and recovery through defined interruptions. This would establish resilience across the complete service.

milestones.label: Patient outcomes meet justified comparison criteria
milestones.explanation: Patient outcomes would have to meet advance criteria against adequately resourced care, accounting for patient and operation risks. This would establish clinical performance.

milestones.label: Independent teams sustain performance with routine local support
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce lasting performance using routine local staffing and maintenance, documenting costs, supplies and surgical access. This would establish practical repeatability.

milestones.label: Published limits identify when additional support is needed
milestones.explanation: Evaluations would have to publish the patients, operations and interruption conditions supported, plus remaining dependencies and referral needs. This would define where the service can be used safely.

uncertain: Which patients and operations should qualify, and how long must dependable performance last?
Which patient outcomes and comparison margins would justify a claim of comparable care?
How much improvement requires new engineering, and how much depends on integrating equipment, training and ongoing support?

page.title: Inhalational anaesthesia during power and oxygen-supply failures
page.definition: An inhalational anaesthesia service—delivering anaesthetic drugs as breathed vapour—maintains WHO–WFSA minimum care standards during mains-power or primary compressed-oxygen failure. It covers assessment through recovery and uses equipment that local technicians can service.

goal.need: The Lancet Commission on Global Surgery’s 2015 estimates quantify unmet need across surgical services. Maintaining anaesthesia during supply failures addresses one constraint on meeting that need; medicines, trained staff and the rest of the surgical service remain necessary.

figures.caption: Unmet surgical need estimated in 2015
rows: People without safe, affordable surgical and anaesthesia care when needed
figures.note: These estimates concern surgical services overall; they do not measure the benefit of an anaesthesia device.

statements.quote: Surgical and anaesthesia care should be an integral component of a national health system in countries at all levels of development.
making quality, safe, effective and affordable emergency and essential surgical care and anaesthesia services accessible to all who need them
statements.context: Resolution WHA68.15 urges Member States to develop financing systems for this purpose.

completion.title: An anaesthesia service meets clinical minimum standards through power and primary oxygen-supply failures.
completion.criterion: An inhalational anaesthesia service meets all applicable WHO–WFSA HIGHLY RECOMMENDED requirements from assessment through recovery during documented mains-power interruptions and primary compressed-oxygen interruptions. Supplemental oxygen continues during general anaesthesia. Equipment permits local servicing. Achievement is limited to the demonstrated patients, procedures and interruption conditions.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas synthesis of WHO–WFSA clinical standards and ISO 8835-7 equipment capabilities.
completion.basis: Searches of WHO–WFSA standards, ISO 8835-7, WFSA tender guidance and UAM trial registrations found no integrated service-level completion test. The Atlas combines published clinical, supply-independence and servicing criteria without adding an outage duration, cost ceiling or clinical non-inferiority margin.

milestones.title: An anaesthetic delivery system operates without mains power or compressed medical gases.
milestones.criterion: Deliver inhalational anaesthesia without mains electricity or compressed medical gases, the capability stated in ISO 8835-7’s scope. In a 75-day Uganda study without patients, one oxygen-storage prototype operating at 0.5–5 L/min covered >99% of 1,284 outages but 56% of 4,295 outage-minutes; this tested oxygen backup alone. A report published on 28 December 2019 describes UAM anaesthesia in 20 Haitian patients, mainly undergoing hernia or hydrocele surgery, without external oxygen or a reliable grid.
milestones.set_by: ISO, ISO 8835-7:2011, published scope; this is its functional capability, not a claim of full conformity.
milestones.threshold_quote: can function in the absence of a supply of compressed medical gases or mains electricity;

milestones.title: Anaesthesia patients receive continuous oximetry and blood-pressure checks usually at least every 5 minutes.
milestones.criterion: Provide continuous pulse oximetry, measuring blood oxygen saturation, and non-invasive blood-pressure checks at appropriate intervals, usually at least every 5 minutes and more frequently if unstable. In Malawi, 83 providers received training and oximeters in August 2014; 66 of 68 located monitors remained in regular use 8 months later. Sixty logbooks contained 4,911 anaesthetics, with 4,772 complete records. The study does not establish compliance with both monitoring requirements.
milestones.set_by: WHO–WFSA, 2018 standards, monitoring section and Table 7.
milestones.threshold_quote: usually at least every five minutes

milestones.title: An anaesthesia service meets all WHO–WFSA minimum requirements from assessment through recovery.
milestones.criterion: Meet every applicable HIGHLY RECOMMENDED requirement in routine care, including assessment, staffing, equipment, medicines, monitoring, checklist use, handover and recovery. At Connaught Hospital, Sierra Leone, a report published on 2 May 2024 describes 287 UAM inhalational cases, uninterrupted anaesthetic delivery during 10 power cuts, and local repair of surge-damaged fuses within hours. Blood pressure was measured in only 612 of 870 post-deployment cases; the report does not establish full clinical compliance.
milestones.set_by: WHO–WFSA, 2018 International Standards for a Safe Practice of Anesthesia.
milestones.threshold_quote: HIGHLY RECOMMENDED standards are the minimum expected standards.

not_found: No retrieved study established full care-pathway compliance during both types of supply interruption.
ISO’s public preview did not expose its normative test clauses.
The WFSA equipment-performance document and its BMJ supplement could not be opened.
The Haiti report’s full text was unavailable on the opened publisher page; its abstract was available.

results.finding: At Connaught Hospital, UAM inhalational anaesthesia continued through 10 power outages.
results.detail: The machine reverted to room air with inhalational anaesthetic, demonstrating delivery without mains power or compressed gas.
results.quote:

results.finding: Among 870 post-deployment cases, providers monitored blood pressure in 612 patients.
results.detail: Pulse oximetry was monitored in 827 patients. The report does not establish continuous oximetry or blood-pressure checks at the required intervals.
results.quote: Providers monitored blood pressure in 612 (70.3%) patients, pulse oximetry in 827 (95.1%), electrocardiography in 30 (3.5%), temperature in 23 (2.7%), and capnography in 10 (1.15%).

results.finding: Among 870 post-deployment cases, providers monitored blood pressure in 612 patients.
results.detail: The observed monitoring gap and incomplete evidence across assessment, care and recovery do not establish all applicable WHO–WFSA requirements.
results.quote: Providers monitored blood pressure in 612 (70.3%) patients, pulse oximetry in 827 (95.1%), electrocardiography in 30 (3.5%), temperature in 23 (2.7%), and capnography in 10 (1.15%).

results.finding: One oxygen-storage prototype covered 56% of outage minutes across 1,284 power outages.
results.detail: The 75-day Uganda study tested oxygen backup at 0.5–5 L/min without patients; it did not demonstrate inhalational anaesthesia delivery.
results.quote: Over the trial period, 1284 power failure episodes with a mean duration of 3.1 minutes (range 0.08 to 1720 minutes) were recorded. The low-pressure system was able to deliver oxygen over 56% of the 4,295 power outage minutes and cover over 99% of power outage events over the course of the study.
